inline.s: Next, meeting the conditions at the end of life, in two [parts]. First, the friend’s guidance. To ‘explain the wonderful Dharma’ is to praise the Pure Land; to ‘instruct him to recite the Buddha’ is to [teach] the [mental] contemplation. (The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Pressed by suffering — the evil signs of hell appear.”) ‘Leisure’ means spare time. Contemplation of the mind [alone] is ‘recitation’; recitation of the mouth is ‘invocation.’ (The Zhizhi Commentary says: “Utterly undivided is called ‘utmost sincerity’; continuing so as to form a whole, hence it never ceases.”) ‘Ten thoughts’ means ten sounds. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘The world always takes invoking the name to be Buddha-recitation; yet the Sūtra says: “That person, pressed by suffering, has no leisure to [contemplate] the Buddha. The good friend says to him: if you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should invoke [his name:] Amitāyus Buddha.” According to this, Buddha-contemplation and name-invocation are clearly different. Before we reach the end-of-life pressing of suffering, besides not abandoning recitation with the mouth, we should also contemplate the Buddha — that is, to bind the mind to it in sustained contemplation. Those who take oral recitation as the exclusive practice and all else as impure [mixed] practice fall into the error of pointing at the finger while mistaking it for the moon!’
By invoking the Buddha’s name, in every thought-moment he removes the karma of birth-and-death for eight billion kalpas.

This clarifies that reciting the Buddha extinguishes offenses. The Zhizhi Commentary says: ‘Question: How is it that ten thoughts can extinguish the offenses of eight billion kalpas? Answer: Because it possesses three powers. First, the power of the originally-inherent Buddha-nature — like fire, like a boat. Second, the power of invoking the name with utmost sincerity — like a drill, like a sail and an oar. These two are the fierce and keen power of one’s own effort. Third, the power of the Buddha’s vow to gather [beings] in — like a person, like a favorable wind. This one is the strong power of another. Since the cause is advantageous, the condition strong, the object sublime, and the mind fierce, [this power] is able to burn up the wood of offense and reach the lotus pond. Dharmākara’s eighteenth vow says: ‘Even [for] ten thoughts, if they are not born [there], I will not attain right enlightenment.’ Again, the Larger Sūtra says: ‘Even to a single thought, with utmost sincerity dedicating [the merit] and vowing to be born in that land, one is immediately reborn.’ The Mahāprajñāpāramitā says: ‘If one person invokes “Namo Buddha,” even to the end of suffering, his merit is not exhausted.’ The Buddha-Name Sūtra says: ‘Upon once hearing the Buddha’s name, one extinguishes the birth-and-death karma of countless kalpas.’ This is like the kindling of a hundred carts of firewood that a single spark can burn; an unlit room of ten thousand years that a single lamp can break through; a single awl piercing a thousand sheets of paper; a single wind [moving] ten million lands. Thus Devadatta, in hell, upon one invocation of the Buddha, transformed manifold suffering into the bliss of the third dhyāna; Zhang Shanhe, before completing ten recitations at death, saw the evil signs destroyed and the Buddha come to welcome him; Zhong Kui set up a Buddha image and removed the suffering of being pecked on the face by a flock of chickens; Xiong Jun, believing in Buddha-recitation, became one who slipped through the net of hell. If a single or three invocations are already thus, how much more ten thoughts and many thoughts?’

The Miao-zong Commentary says: ‘This fierce and keen mind arises from two conditions: first, encountering a good friend; second, being pressed by suffering. The mind fears the evil destinies, and the ear hears the Buddha’s name; hence it is firm and strong and invokes with utmost sincerity. Since the object is sublime and the mind fierce, little time [yields] great merit, able to surpass the drifting vow-power of a hundred years. If these two conditions do not arouse a fierce mind, this person is one who should fall into hell.’

At the moment of death he sees a golden lotus, like the orb of the sun, standing before him. In a single thought-moment he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within the lotus, for a full twelve great kalpas, the flower opens. Then Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of great compassion, explain at length to him the reality of all dharmas and the method that extinguishes offenses. Having heard it, he rejoices and in that very moment arouses the bodhi-mind. This is the lower-birth of the lower grade.

Next, the excellent sign appears. The flower being like the sun’s orb is a simile for its size. If one follows the Abhidharma-kośa, the sun’s disk is fifty-one yojanas in diameter; here it merely takes what [beings] dwelling on earth look up to see — the size is not necessarily as [that] treatise [states]. Below ‘in a single thought-moment’ [the text] clarifies the gaining of rebirth. Below ‘within the lotus’ [it clarifies] the benefits after rebirth. Offenses arise from conditions and have no self-nature; all dharmas are likewise, hence [the truth] is called ‘reality.’ The Samantabhadra Practice says: ‘All the seas of karmic hindrances arise from false thinking; if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality’ — this is [the point]. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.) The Yanyi commentary says: ‘This grade is especially long! It takes twelve great kalpas before the lotus opens. The flower opens and the hindrances are cleared away, like the clouds parting and the sky clearing. [He] hears the two great bodhisattvas explaining at length the wonderful Dharma. As for “the reality of all dharmas” — this means pointing to ignorance as the wonderful brightness, realizing the deluded awareness as true awareness, making clear that all dharmas are in their very essence reality.

… “All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them” — this is no idle saying. Therefore in that very moment he arouses the bodhi-mind.’ With this the last sentence concludes [the section].
This is called the lower-class-rebirth contemplation; it is the sixteenth contemplation.”

The Shi-lun Commentary says: ‘Among the lower grade, only the upper-birth one, after ten small kalpas, attains entry into the first stage; the other two are not described as to their fruition — they are presumably of the class of devas and humans in the Pure Land.’

The Yue-lun Commentary says: ‘The text of the nine grades, collectively called “contemplations,” is so that the practitioner may possess the wisdom of discernment and arouse a mind of vigor; to forsake the lower and rise to the higher, to turn away from the small and direct toward the great; and also that he may know that, upheld by the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, no gift [of capacity] is left unspread.’ With this, [the commentary] explains the meaning of ‘contemplation’ from the standpoint of the cause of practice. If one distinguishes by way of the fruit, it is entirely as said before. As for clarifying the [spiritual] stages, the Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘According to the Profound Meaning of the Four-Fascicle Commentary, the masters of old all used the three worthies and ten sages of the Great Vehicle to correspond to the upper three grades; the two kinds of [ordinary beings and] the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle to correspond to the middle three grades; and the beginning-learners, ordinary people of the Great Vehicle, according to the gravity of their offenses, to correspond to the lower three grades. That passage (meaning the Profound Meaning division of the Four-Fascicle Commentary) refutes [these opinions] at length, and I do not quote it all again. Now I hold: according to the text of the nine grades, it is after being reborn in that land that the stages are discussed, so [the masters] may be followed. And according to the scripture text, those who seek rebirth from this world are all ordinary people; one must follow the Profound Meaning.

…’ The Profound Meaning of the Four-Fascicle Commentary says: ‘The overall purport of the three classes of the Contemplation Sūtra, above and below, is always [the case of] ordinary people in the five turbidities after the Buddha’s passing. Only because they meet different conditions are the nine grades made to differ. Why? The three of the upper grade are ordinary people who meet the Great [Vehicle]; the three of the middle grade are ordinary people who meet the Small [Vehicle]; the three of the lower grade are ordinary people who meet evil [conditions]. Because of their evil karma, at the end of life they rely on a good [friend] and, riding the power of the Buddha’s vows, are able to be reborn; only on reaching [that land] and [the time of the] flower’s opening do they arouse the mind. How can it be said that they are people who are beginning to study the Great Vehicle? …’ The details are in the commentary; the text is lengthy and is not transcribed.
Yi 3: The assembly benefits [from hearing]

While he was speaking these words, Vaidehī and the five hundred maidservants, hearing what the Buddha said, at once beheld the wide and long features of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; they saw the Buddha’s body and the two bodhisattvas. Their minds were filled with joy and they exclaimed at what had never been before! They awakened with sudden comprehension and attained the patience of non-arising. The five hundred maidservants aroused the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and vowed to be born in that land. The World-Honored One prophesied of them all: they would all be reborn there. Having been born in that land, they would obtain the samādhi of the Buddhas appearing before them. Countless devas aroused the unsurpassed bodhi-mind.

The text [has] two [sections]. First, the assembly sees the pure adornments of the dependent and the proper [retribution] of that land. Previously only Vaidehī alone saw it; now the whole assembly beholds it. Next, below ‘their minds,’ according to capacity they obtain benefits — in three [parts]. First, the queen enters realization. She ‘awakened with sudden comprehension’ — destroying ignorance; she ‘attained the patience of non-arising’ — realizing the Dharma-nature. Second, below ‘the five hundred,’ the maidservants arouse the mind and receive the prophecy. Question: The Treatise on Rebirth says that women and those with defective faculties are all unable to be born [there] — how is this not contradicted here? Answer: It does not say that the women of this world and those with defective faculties cannot be born in that land; it means that those who are born in that land do not receive the retribution of being a woman or of defective faculties. For Amitabha vowed: ‘If any woman, having come to be born in my land, again receives the form of a woman, I will not attain right enlightenment.’ It further says: ‘If any of the humans and devas of my land do not possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, I will not attain right enlightenment.’ From this one knows that in that land there are no women nor defective faculties. The rest is as explained in the Ten Doubts Treatise. Third, below ‘countless,’ the devas arouse the mind. The Buddha, in the secluded palace, spoke this method of contemplation with Ānanda and Maudgalyāyana attending at his side. There were only the queen, the maidservants, and the devas as the audience — no others heard it. Later, returning to Vulture Peak, Ānanda repeated it, and only then did the great assembly of bodhisattvas together hear it. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

blocks.text: Jia 3: The section of the Propagation — in two parts

inline.s: First, at the palace in the royal city, entrusting the propagation
second, returning to Vulture Peak, Ānanda retells it
The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘Through these two places, the assembly hears, believes, and accepts; transmitted and handed on from one to another, it flows without end.’
Yi 1: At the palace in the royal city, entrusting the propagation — in four parts
First, establishing the name and teaching its upholding
second, raising the benefits and urging the practice; third, concluding the name and entrusting it; fourth, the assembly hears and rejoices
Bing 1: Establishing the name and teaching its upholding
At that time Ānanda rose from his seat, and said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One! By what name should this Sūtra be known? And how should the essentials of this Dharma be received and upheld?’
First, Ānanda’s two questions about the name and the upholding. First, he asks the name of the Sūtra; second, he asks the method of upholding.

The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘This Sūtra is called the Contemplation of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, of Amitāyus Buddha, of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, and of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. It is also called the Complete Purification of Karmic Obstructions and Being Born before the Buddhas. You should receive and uphold it, and let it not be lost.

Next, within the Buddha’s answer, first, setting forth the name of the Sūtra. There are two [aspects]. First, the name is taken from the one who contemplates and the object contemplated; it includes both the [three] objects [of contemplation], but omits the assembly. The opening title avoids prolixity and takes only five characters, yet its inclusiveness is complete. Second, [the name] is taken from its function. The extinguishing of offenses and [the bringing about of] rebirth are the power and use of the Sūtra. Second, below ‘you should uphold,’ [the Buddha] teaches its upholding. The Treatise on Wisdom says: Through the power of faith one receives; through the power of mindfulness one upholds. Having both received and upheld, one does not forget or lose it. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Bing 2: Raising the benefits and urging the practice

Those who practice this samādhi, in this very life, see Amitāyus Buddha and the two great bodhisattvas. If good men and good women merely hear the name of that Buddha and the names of the two bodhisattvas, they remove the karma of birth-and-death for countless kalpas — how much more so if they recollect [them]. If one practices Buddha-recitation, know that such a person is the puṇḍarīka (white lotus) among humans. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva are his excellent companions. He will sit at the place of enlightenment and be born in the family of the Buddhas.’

The text [has] five [points]. First, the excellence of the object seen. The [chapter on] Mahasthamaprapta’s perfect penetration says: ‘If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha, whether now [in this life] or in the future, they will certainly see the Buddha.’ Second, below ‘merely hear,’ the excellence of extinguishing offenses. To cite [the mere] hearing to make [the case for] recollection — its superiority is knowable. Third, below ‘if one practices,’ the excellence of the person himself. ‘Puṇḍarīka’ is here [rendered] ‘white lotus.’ First, it is a rare auspicious [flower] in the human world; second, its nature is pure and free of defilement — hence it is used as the comparison. Fourth, below ‘Avalokiteshvara,’ the excellence of companions. To have a Buddha-to-be as a friend, it is fitting not to slight oneself. Fifth, below ‘he will sit,’ the excellence of the retribution. ‘Sitting at the place of enlightenment’ means becoming a Buddha. The place where the way is attained is therefore called the ‘place of enlightenment.’ All the Buddhas, beneath the bodhi tree, sit cross-legged, cut off defilements, defeat the Māras, and attain the way. The Dharma-body is one substance, realized alike by all Buddhas, hence [they are] of the ‘Buddha family.’ The Mahasthamaprapta chapter says ‘Not far from the Buddha,’ and the Smaller Sūtra says all of them attain the non-regressing anuttara [bodhi] — these point to the same meaning. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Bing 3: Concluding the name and entrusting it
The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘Uphold these words well; one who upholds these words is hereby upholding the Name of Amitāyus Buddha.’
The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘The intent is to state by way of contrast: the merit of upholding the Name is great, and so too is upholding the Sūtra.’
Bing 4: The assembly hears and rejoices
When the Buddha spoke these words, the venerable Maudgalyāyana, the venerable Ānanda, and Vaidehī and the rest, hearing what the Buddha said, all rejoiced greatly.

The Ling-zhi Commentary says: ‘As for “rejoicing”: first, [what they] had never heard before, they now hear it; second, they are able to be reborn in the pure land; third, [this teaching] can be shown and explained on and on, benefiting living beings without end. Possessing all these meanings, they hold great joy.’
Yi 2: Returning to Vulture Peak, Ānanda retells it
At that time the World-Honored One, treading in the sky, returned to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).

First, the Buddha returns to his place. Since the Buddha spoke the Sūtra for a long time in the royal palace, either the assembly did not disperse and waited for the Buddha to return, or they gathered again — neither can be known. (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)

At that time Ānanda explained at length to the great assembly the matters as above. Countless devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, hearing what the Buddha said, all rejoiced greatly; and, paying reverence to the Buddha, they withdrew.

Next, Ānanda retells it. The repeated entrusting to remember and uphold [the Sūtra] — its purport appears here. Third, the assembly hears, does reverence, and disperses. Referring to the assembly listed above, the text here abbreviates the nāgas and devas. Ānanda himself heard [it] and, on behalf [of the Buddha], transmitted the Buddha’s words — hence it says ‘hearing the Buddha say [this].’ (The Ling-zhi Commentary.)
Completed as the first draft, on the morning of the day before the Buddha’s birthday, in the xinchou year of the Republic of China, in the Huayan retreat.
